extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and law students studying preliminary injunction practice
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and factors courts use when deciding whether to grant a preliminary injunction in patent cases, especially the evidentiary weight to be given to prior judgments, public acquiescence, admissions, identity of parties/issues, and availability of testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment sustaining patent is evidence of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: That a judgment sustaining the patent is evidence of its validity for the purposes of an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judgment in favor of a patent is strong evidence at a preliminary hearing; courts often treat such judgments as creating a presumption of validity, sometimes so strong that others are not allowed to contradict it. (Cited examples: Putnam v. Keystone Co.; Stuart v. Thorman.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Public acquiescence supports patent validity
rubrics_metrics.description: That acquiescence in the monopoly is evidence to prove the validity of the patent on a motion for an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long public acceptance, licenses, long enjoyment, or frequent recoveries support a patent's validity and make injunctive relief more likely; public acquiescence is one of the most weighty non-judicial forms of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions by defendant may substitute for judgments/acquiescence
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissions by the defendant acknowledging or implying acknowledgment that the patent is valid may be received as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such admissions can supply the place of judgments and acquiescence and are considered when both judicial and public corroboration are absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of prior judgments depends on circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The weight to be attached to any judgment in favor of a patent as evidence of its validity depends upon the circumstances under which it was rendered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include identity of parties, identity of issues, identity/equivalence of testimony, authority of the tribunal, whether the defendant was interested in prior defenses, whether the prior proceeding was contested, and whether new evidence exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated judgments sustaining patent increase probability of injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will be granted on proof of infringement only if the patent has been sustained by repeated judgments, especially where the defendant was interested in prior defenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple favorable adjudications create a strong presumption; courts have issued injunctions where the patent had been repeatedly upheld (see Robertson v. Hill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Short remaining patent term not a bar where validity sustained
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will issue where a patent has but a short time to run and has been fully sustained by judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even limited remaining term will not prevent injunctive relief if validity and infringement are clear (Cary v. Domestic Spring Bed Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction may issue under extension or reissue depending on original support
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will issue under an extension if the original had been sustained and other supporting circumstances exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will consider whether original patent had been sustained, extended, or reissued and whether the reissue broadens claims; careful inquiry needed when reissues are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: No injunction where patent not adjudicated and patentability doubtful
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will be refused where the patent has not been adjudicated and patentability is doubtful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior judgments are absent and there is genuine doubt about patentability (e.g., Baldwin v. Conway), courts may deny preliminary relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long acquiescence + judgments + clear infringement favor injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will be granted if there has been long acquiescence in the patent, judgments sustaining it, and clear infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combination of these factors (acquiescence, adjudications, clear infringement) strongly supports injunctive relief (Schneider v. Missouri Glass Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses, Office examination, and a neighbor-circuit judgment support injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where many licenses had been taken, the invention fully examined in the Patent Office, and a judgment rendered in its favor in a neighboring circuit, an injunction may be issued even if defendant's injury would be trifling compared to plaintiff's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These indicia of de facto acceptance and scrutiny of the patent bolster the plaintiff's case at the preliminary stage (Hat Sweat Mfg. Co. v. Davis Sewing Mach. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: No injunction absent judgment/acquiescence unless plaintiff's right clear
rubrics_metrics.description: No injunction will issue where there has been neither long exclusive possession, nor any judgment, nor irreparable injury, unless the plaintiff shows a clear and unquestionable right or exclusive possession raising a presumption of such right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require either strong equitable indicators or clear proof of rights before granting preliminary relief; otherwise plaintiff must first obtain a trial at law (Thomas v. Weeks; Earth Closet Co. v. Fenner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Where patent sustained only by acquiescence, infringement must be palpable
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent is sustained only by acquiescence, no injunction will issue unless the infringement is palpable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliance solely on acquiescence is weaker than judicial adjudication; courts require clear proof of infringement in such situations (Burleigh Rock Drill Co. v. Lobdell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of parties/privies required for preclusive effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity of parties is a question for the court; both parties and privies are concluded by a judgment, and persons who employed counsel or paid expenses may be treated as parties or privies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look beyond named parties to those who controlled or participated in litigation (employing counsel, funding). Privies must have had the ability to control litigation (motions, evidence, appeal) to be bound (Miller v. Liggett & Myers; United States v. Foreign Salamander Felting Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Privy must have had control of litigation to be bound
rubrics_metrics.description: A privy to be concluded must be such that he can control the litigation by making motions, offering evidence, examining witnesses, and taking appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely peripheral association is insufficient; active control or direction is required for preclusion (Miller v. Liggett & Myers).

rubrics_metrics.name: A judgment is precedent only upon issues decided
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgment is a precedent only upon the issues which it expressly, or by necessary implication, has determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior litigation did not decide the specific issue now raised (e.g., different claims, reissue claims, or different defenses), those matters remain open. Courts demand that the prior judgment either show on its face or be supported by testimony proving it decided the same issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of issues, testimony, and tribunal authority affect precedential weight
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgment of a court of last resort in a suit between the same parties on the same issues and same or equivalent evidence is conclusive; the decision of an inferior tribunal in different litigation is of slight or no importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher-court adjudications carry greater persuasive/mandatory force; lower-court or differently-framed adjudications have limited weight unless the facts and issues substantially coincide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior judgment may be avoided by showing it did not decide relevant points or material facts were unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of a former judgment may be avoided by showing that the plaintiff's title was not then in controversy, or that some material fact was then unknown or overlooked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant can introduce extrinsic evidence or new facts to show the prior adjudication did not actually decide the point now asserted (Parker v. Brant; National Hat Pouncing Mach. Co. v. Hedden).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior judgment's weight reduced by new or additional evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: New and additional evidence on the same points may deprive a former judgment of its weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may hear testimony anew and decide de novo if convinced that error was committed or material new evidence exists (Lockwood & Faber).

rubrics_metrics.name: Where prior judgment does not show which claims were held valid, scope remains open
rubrics_metrics.description: If a former judgment does not show which claims of the patent were held valid, both the scope of the patent and the fact of infringement are open for inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly where multiple claims or multiple patents were involved, a court on a motion for a preliminary injunction should require proof of which specific claim was adjudicated (Russell v. Place; Cobum v. Clark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/construction points may be treated as settled across parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain matters relating to validity governed by rules of legal definition and construction — e.g., whether an invention results from inventive skill, class protected by statute, whether reissue claims are identical, formal sufficiency, and what the patent claims — once carefully decided may be regarded as permanently settled for future litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike fact-contingent issues, pure legal questions and constructions have broader precedential effect and will often be followed by other courts (Treatise discussion in §1179).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-dependent issues not binding on others
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions contingent upon evidence — priority, novelty, utility, abandonment, sufficiency of the description, or the inventor's good faith — are not properly treated as conclusively established by prior judgments between different parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such issues depend heavily on presented evidence; other parties should not be prejudiced by an imperfect presentation of those facts in earlier litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit courts guided by prior decisions only when same questions and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Circuit courts follow prior decisions where the same questions are in controversy or raised on the same evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial comity leads courts to respect prior constructions, but only to the extent the factual/evidentiary posture matches (Edgarton v. Furst & Bradley Mfg. Co.; Spring v. Domestic Sewing Mach. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court judgments are plenary proof between same parties/issues
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgment of the Supreme Court of the United States is binding on all other courts until reversed or modified; its decision that a patent is valid must be received as plenary proof of such validity between the same parties and on the same issues, absent fraud or newly discovered evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower courts must follow Supreme Court determinations of law; validity determinations have great force but can be attacked only for fraud or material new evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior uncontested judgments carry less weight
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgment obtained without contest on several patents is not of as much weight as if only the one now in question had been sued on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a judgment resulted from an uncontested or poorly contested proceeding (e.g., several patents/lots were surrendered), its value as precedent or proof for a later preliminary injunction is diminished (Grover & Baker Sewing Mach. Co. v. Williams).

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts require careful inquiry before using indefinite prior orders as basis for injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary injunctions should not be based on indefinite or perfunctory prior orders that may have ostensibly covered many claims; courts should require explicit showing of what claim was held valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A more searching inquiry is needed for preliminary injunctions than a mere perfunctory order possibly covering all claims; otherwise defendants may suffer destructive prejudice (Coburn v. Clark).
